html:
The Apinajé are a Jê-speaking people of northern Tocantins in Brazil, near where the Araguaia River meets the Tocantins. They belong to the Timbira group of the north-eastern Jê, kin of the Canela.

Like other Jê peoples of the savanna, they lived in large circular villages, with houses ringed around a central plaza where ceremonies and councils took place. They farmed, hunted and gathered, and are known for log races, in which teams carry heavy logs. Their social life, with its paired halves and age groups, was described by the ethnographer Curt Nimuendajú in the 1930s, a classic of anthropology. Settlers, roads and cattle ranches from the 1800s onward took much of their land, but they keep a territory today in Brazil.
